label: Claude Haiku 5.5
output:
11 November 2026

Kelechi,

Before you start laughing at me for posting you a letter, yes, I know. You said put it in writing, so I'm putting it in writing, with a stamp on it, which you will tell everyone is extra.

Let me start with the bit you'll hate most, so you can't say I didn't. Teaching is hard. My first year I cried in the staff car park twice in the same term. Once was after a lesson that went completely sideways, and once was on a Tuesday for no reason I could name. The marking never ends. There's a pile on my desk on Friday night that's still there on Sunday evening. Some days behaviour is wahala, and you spend the whole lesson managing a room instead of teaching it. I'm not going to pretend otherwise, because you'd smell it from Croydon.

The pay drops in your training year. Yes. You check other people's costings for a living, so you already know the numbers better than I do, and I'm not going to talk you round them. But the holidays are proper holidays, not annual leave with a conversation attached. The pension is decent. The salary goes up after that first year and keeps going, so the dip is one year, not a permanent new normal. Put it in a spreadsheet. You'll see it.

Now the bit I actually want you to think about.

Last month a Year 11 boy, Damola, finally got simultaneous equations. He'd spent three weeks convinced he was "just not a maths person." He sat there looking at his working, went quiet, and then shouted "is that all??" and the whole class clapped. Nobody told them to. He'd earned it. I wish you could have seen his face. I've been doing this seven years and that still gets me.

And think about Christmas. You sat with my nephew and did fractions with jollof rice on plates, halves and quarters, and he still talks about it. He told everyone "Uncle Kelechi's rice" for a month. You didn't make him feel stupid. You never make anyone feel stupid. You never could. Even in Moremi, when half the hostel was queuing outside your room before exams, you'd explain integration for the fourth time without once making anyone feel thick. That patience is the actual skill, and you already have it. Training is mostly learning to point it at thirty teenagers at once instead of six people who owe you money for jollof.

There's a woman in my department who started at 41. She's brilliant. Your 34 is not old. Stop it.

On your last birthday you said, "I just want to do something that matters before I'm 40." I've thought about that more than you'd guess. You said it, then changed the subject quickly, because you hate sounding serious. I heard it anyway. I'm not saying you're some lost soul. You're a good quantity surveyor, nine years in, and you're good at it. It's still a spreadsheet every day, and you're allowed to be bored of that. Being bored at 34 isn't a crisis. Being bored at 44 might be.

I'm not asking you to sign anything. I'm not asking you to quit or to decide by Christmas. I'm asking you to come to the open evening on Thursday 19 November, 6pm, at the training partnership in Lewisham. I'll come with you. Afterwards I'll buy you a proper dinner, and you can interrogate every teacher in the room the way you interrogate contractors. Ask them about the marking. Ask them about the bad days. Ask them what they wish someone had told them before they started. If it's rubbish, you'll know, and I'll buy the dinner anyway and never mention it again. (I'll mention it again.)

Applications open soon and you can take your time. The route starts September 2027. Nothing has to happen before then except you walking into one room and seeing what it's like.

I know you'll read this on the train and say Aidan has written an essay. I have. You asked for a proper letter, and this is it. Consider it a deposit.

See you on the 19th. Wear something warm, and don't come in with that face you do when someone says "synergy."

Aidan

---

Posting it: the open evening is eight days away, so send it first class or by Royal Mail Special Delivery if you want to be sure it lands before the 19th. A standard second-class letter from Peckham to Croydon can take two or three days, which should still be fine, but there's not much slack.
